title: False-positive triage
text: A false positive is an alert that labels benign activity as malicious. Threat intelligence indicators require context because a shared address or a reused domain can serve both legitimate and malicious users. Analysts should review the observation time, affected asset, source reliability, and supporting evidence before blocking an indicator. Expired indicators can continue to generate alerts long after a threat has disappeared. An allowlist can reduce repeated benign alerts, but each exception needs an owner, an explanation, and an expiry date. Triage should record both the decision and its evidence so another analyst can review the reasoning. A low confidence score alone does not prove an event is benign. Independent telemetry, such as endpoint logs and authentication records, helps confirm whether an alert reflects real compromise. Measure false-positive rates only when reliable truth labels exist. Without labels, describe suspected false positives as review candidates rather than confirmed mistakes.

title: Source reputation and freshness
text: Source reputation estimates how reliably a threat intelligence provider reports useful indicators. Reputation should consider historical validation, reporting delay, coverage, and correction practices. Several providers may copy the same upstream feed, so many repeated reports do not necessarily represent independent evidence. Analysts should preserve provider identity and observation timestamps when combining feeds. Fresh evidence deserves investigation, but recency does not guarantee accuracy. Old indicators can still be relevant when a campaign persists. Review whether an indicator belongs to shared infrastructure, a content delivery network, or a commonly used hosting service before assigning blame. Correlating multiple independent sources can strengthen a finding when they agree on the same behavior and time window. Track both true positives and false positives after analyst review. Avoid suppressing every event from a low-rated source because that can hide emerging threats. Confidence should be documented alongside uncertainty and updated as new evidence arrives.

title: Phishing investigations
text: Phishing attempts deceive users into revealing credentials or opening malicious content. An investigation can start with a suspicious email, a newly observed domain, or an unexpected login page. Analysts examine message headers, destination URLs, domain registration context, and the relationship between the claimed sender and the actual infrastructure. Users should report the message through the approved channel instead of interacting with unknown links. A security team can compare the reported domain with known business services and review authentication logs for account compromise. If credentials were exposed, reset the affected credentials and revoke active sessions according to the incident procedure. Strong multi-factor authentication can reduce some credential abuse, but analysts still need to examine session theft and other bypass techniques. Not every unusual domain is malicious. Record the evidence, preserve the original report, and avoid making a final conclusion from a single indicator.

title: Ransomware response
text: Ransomware disrupts access to data and can also involve theft of sensitive files. Detection may combine unusual file modifications, unexpected process execution, abnormal network traffic, and reports from affected users. A response team should isolate affected hosts according to the incident plan, preserve relevant logs, identify the scope of impact, and coordinate recovery with authorized staff. Verified offline or immutable backups can help restore service, but restoration must follow containment so the same threat does not immediately return. Analysts should check whether the apparent file activity comes from legitimate backup or encryption software before treating every event as malicious. Correlating endpoint telemetry with threat intelligence supports a more reliable decision. Record timestamps carefully to reconstruct the incident sequence. Recovery tests should verify data integrity and application behavior. A generated answer from a language model is supporting information, not a substitute for an approved incident response procedure.

title: Evidence correlation and graph analysis
text: Correlation joins observations from several systems to explain an event. A threat graph can connect sources, indicators, targets, and time windows. Dense connections may reveal a coordinated campaign, but they can also result from benign shared hosting or several feeds copying the same information. Graph communities therefore identify groups for review rather than automatically proving fraud or false positives. Analysts should cross-reference the graph with the original event records and check how relationships were constructed. A shared target is weaker evidence than a shared target observed with the same suspicious behavior at a relevant time. Preserve source provenance so copied reports are not counted as independent confirmations. Use clear rules to select candidates, and record the rule version in the report. Evaluate detection quality on labeled examples whenever possible. Query latency and graph density alone do not measure the accuracy of a threat classification. Human review remains necessary for decisions with operational impact.
